Where it began

Monty Panesar was born in Luton on 25 April 1982, and he is a Luton Town supporter. He went to Stopsley High School, then to Bedford Modern School for the sixth form, and later took a degree in computer science at Loughborough University.

He started out as a medium-pace bowler. At around sixteen, during a school coaching session, the former Northamptonshire seamer Paul Taylor told him to try spin instead. He made his first-class debut for Northamptonshire in 2001, aged 19, and after graduating took 51 County Championship wickets in 2005.

The player

England picked him for the tour of India early in 2006, and in his first Test, at Nagpur, his first wicket was Sachin Tendulkar, his boyhood hero. Tendulkar later signed the ball and gave it to him. In all he played 50 Tests between 2006 and 2013 and took 167 wickets at 34.71, with 12 five-wicket innings and two ten-wicket matches.

At Perth in 2006–07 he became the first English spinner to take five wickets in a Test innings at the WACA. Against West Indies at Old Trafford in 2007 he took ten in a match, something no English spinner had done since Phil Tufnell in 1997, and he was man of the series with 23 wickets. Then, in India in late 2012, he took 11 for 210 in the second Test, the first time an English spinner had taken ten in a match there since Hedley Verity in 1934, and England went on to win a series in India for the first time since 1984–85.

What made him special

He had unusually large hands and a wrist that could turn a full circle, which gave the ball plenty of work. Andrew Strauss, who captained him, described a man who was first to arrive at practice and last to leave.

Batting and fielding came less naturally. Crowds famously cheered even his simplest stops, and his Test batting average was 4.89. Yet he had his moments: a brisk 26 against Sri Lanka in 2006 that included a six off Murali, and the last 40 minutes at Cardiff in 2009, when he and James Anderson blocked out 69 balls to save the first Ashes Test.

Away from the middle

Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 2007. In January 2017 Cricket Australia took him on as a spin-bowling consultant for their tour of India. He wrote an autobiography, The Full Monty, published in 2019, and studied sports journalism at St Mary's University in London. He also kept playing club cricket well into his forties, signing for Great Witchingham for 2024 and for Pelsall in 2026.

And finally

Early in his England days the commentator Henry Blofeld once called him Monty Python by mistake on air. Before long The Python had joined his long list of nicknames, surely one of the few nicknames in cricket handed out entirely by accident.
